audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht Biomedical Sciences studies the human body in health and disease. The programme builds from cells, molecules, tissues and organ systems to laboratory and data methods. Students choose biomedical electives and complete a supervised research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The three UCR options emphasise broad biomedical science, molecular genetics and computational methods, or human physiology and mental health. They share laboratory and disease-focused study. Utrecht requires a dedicated bioinformatics course and an experimental project with a thesis.

curriculum.limitation: This outline shows the standard 15 EC research project and preserves the official biomedical electives and 45 EC of profiling space.

componentNotes.bmw-y1-choice: Choose from the first-year biomedical electives, which include ethics, evolutionary biology, introductory neuroscience and medical imaging.
componentNotes.bmw-major-choice: Complete at least five courses from the ten-course major list, including Moleculaire Biologie van de Cel. Major and degree-level requirements apply.
componentNotes.bmw-research: The standard 15 EC project combines a literature study, experimental work, an English thesis and a research-integrity module. Entry requires 150 EC. A 22.5 EC Plus option is available under separate rules.
componentNotes.bmw-profiling: At least 15 of these 45 EC must be at level 2 or 3. Course-entry and overlap rules apply.

notes.text: Utrecht requires an integrated biomedical major and a supervised research project with an English thesis. UCR offers molecular and human biology, laboratory methods, and quantitative and behavioural study. The UCR options provide preparation in these areas, while Utrecht requires dedicated bioinformatics and project-based research.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

HCBGATE101.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
HCBGATE101.text: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Topics include biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, metabolism, cell division, heredity, gene expression and biotechnology. Students analyse scientific experiments and papers through teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium, with additional topics selected with the class.

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.text: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

HCBBIOM111.text: Introduces epidemiology and the evidence used in public health. It examines disease patterns, risks and changes over time, and how research can inform decisions about population health.

HCBCOGN112.text: Neurobiology studies nervous systems and behaviour through comparative anatomy, evolution and physiology. Students examine animal behaviour, research models, welfare and research ethics, then connect biological rhythms and regulatory behaviour to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based report apply neurobiological concepts.

Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models for group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.

Medical images, anatomical drawing, human-specimen material and guided practicals develop spatial reasoning, including observation in a dissection room. GOSPHIL212.text: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel.
